utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom and everyone in Sweden. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, including the persons in Bosnia who are hearing us via videolink and telephone. May we have the appearances please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, in Sweden. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Office of the Prosecutor, Gerard Dobbyn, with Tom Hannis, Indah Susanti, and our Legal Intern Catherine Loftus.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I was just standing to adjust the volume. But we are ready to call our next witness who is ST-244. He has protective measures in the form of a pseudonym and image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. I trust that you can hear me, Mr. Court Officer, and that the witness is available. Could you have him, first of all, make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, good morning, Your Honours. Good morning. I can hear you in a language we understand. And the witness is present. Should I bring him in front of the camera?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Witness. Would you please confirm that you can hear me in a language that you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would, first of all, invite you to make the solemn declaration on the card that the Court Officer will hand to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We should move into private session, having regard to the protective measures that are in place in respect of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. And I apologise, Your Honours, the pseudonym sheet will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, moving to late 1991, early 1992, did you ever hear about the existence of parallel Serbian government structures in Prijedor municipality prior to the Serbian takeover of power in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the takeover of power, or, rather, earlier than that, I did not have any premonition that something like that would happen. However, later, in the spring of 1992, I heard on the radio and from some other people that there was an announcement on Radio Prijedor that a Serbian municipality or Serbian Municipal Assembly, Serbian Executive Committees were formed, but I didn't know about that earlier. I heard about that from others and on the radio. That was maybe a month before the takeover of power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to April 1992 - again, before the takeover - were you aware of a meeting in Prijedor in which the staffing of police was discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of that meeting, and I heard that the chief of police from Banja Luka was present at the public security station in Prijedor where the meeting was held, although I didn't attend. I heard that there was discussion about regionalisation and of moving to -- the police into the region of the Serbian Krajina, that uniforms would be changed, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now when you say that the chief of police from Banja Luka was present, do you know that person's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Stojan Zupljanin was chief of police of Banja Luka at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear whether there was any specific discussion about appointment of certain individuals to positions within the police in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that at that meeting, although I wasn't present, I heard of it, and I heard that there was discussion about annexing it to the Serbian region. As far as the leadership of the police is concerned, there were the commander of police and other high executive positions, and this is the area where the SDS created the greatest problems with respect to the appointments to these positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just very briefly, could you describe what sort of problems the SDS were creating in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For example, the former president of SDS in Prijedor, Srdjo Srdic, I happened to be at the meeting with the president of the executive committee, the late Kovacevic, when Srdic was there, prior to the appointment of the chief of police in Prijedor and the commander of police. Srdic said as follows: If the things were not done according to their proposal, a war will break out in Prijedor and that will serve as a tool to serve all the issues and problems that hadn't been solved during the Second World War as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm going to move on and asking you some questions about what you experienced during the Serb takeover of Prijedor at the end of April 1992. And, first of all, I'd like to ask you, did you go into work on the day of the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look, nobody expected us -- actually, none of us expected that to happen. That was a normal and usual day for me. I was getting ready to go to work, and at that point the then-chief of police Talundjic called me by phone and asked me what I was doing. I said I was getting ready to work. He said, There's no need for you to go because in Prijedor the Serbian SDS had taken power and they posted guards in front of the municipal building and all other important facilities, such as the bank, the public auditing office, et cetera, so he said that there were armed people everywhere. So on that day it was impossible to go to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see for yourself whether there were, in fact, armed people on the streets in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I was able to see them. I could see from my window both armed men on the move but also some guards posted outside the SDS headquarters. And, of course, I also saw from my window a large number of armed people dressed in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall if there were any announcements over the radio at that time regarding the employment of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, this is how it happened: First of all, but specifically later, each company or work organisation either dismissed their workers or they simply refused the non-Serbs to continue working. Then later, when they were unable to come and they wanted to see some people in positions, there was an announcement on the radio that everybody must come to their respective places of work. And I think that was one of the ways to effect arrests of those who hadn't already been arrested. They were invited to come to their workplace and then they would conduct interviews there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now just moving to the first few days after the takeover. Do you know if any non-Serbs remained in any political positions or any positions in the municipal government in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, starting from the Executive Board of the municipality, none of the elected people elected in the elections remained in office. As for the companies, I know that there were some such cases. Some people reported for work. And I know that there were some people who were at the head of the SIZ, the so-called SIZ for refugees and things like that. And I know that the Executive Committee quickly changed that. This new Executive Committee, which in my eyes was illegal, decided to replace those individuals. For example, that applied to the deputy or the public defender or the president of the Red Cross organisation, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the removal of non-Serbs from political positions and these other positions you've referred to, who replaced them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't find out that immediately because I had very scarce information at the time. However, later, I heard that those were the people thought to be suitable by the SDS, meaning the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, whether non-Serbs who were being dismissed from these positions were given any explanation for their dismissals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, these people who were dismissed, at least for some of them, I know that they went to Omarska and they were -- they died there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask that particular question again. When -- when people were dismissed or told not to come into work, was any explanation given as to why they were not to come in to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. For example, in my case, or anybody else in the Executive Committee were not provided any explanation, nor did anybody consider that they should give us an explanation, simply because we were non-Serbs. We were Bosniaks. And I believe that those people who were in responsible positions were not asked and were not told why they had been replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, at this point I'd like to call up 65 ter 3687. And this is in tab 7 of the Prosecution's binder of documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I can't see you. Do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll see that this is a decision of the Executive Committee of the Serbian municipality of Prijedor. It's dated the 4th of May, 1992. And it's signed and stamped for Dr. Milan Kovacevic as president of the Executive Committee. And you can see also that this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll see that this decision states that Esad Mehmedagic is dismissed from the post of deputy municipal public attorney and that Slobodan Radulj is appointed acting municipal public attorney. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, do you know the ethnicity of these two people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man who is being dismissed is a Bosniak, and the person being appointed is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And this man, Mr. Mehmedagic, who was dismissed, do you know what subsequently happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, and this later became official, Mehmedagic ended up at Omarska and unfortunately he died. He was unable to move on his own because he was very, very, short-sighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01738, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd now like to move on to another document. If we could call up 65 ter 3684. And this is in tab 4 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have this document in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, just one little follow-up question to the witness. Mr. Witness, you said that Mr. Mehmedagic unfortunately died. Did he died at Omarska or did he die -- when did he die and where did he die; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, based on things I heard and read, he died at Omarska in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the document you have in front you now is another decision of the Executive Committee of the Serbian municipality of Prijedor. This one's dated 5th of May, 1992, and appears to be signed by Dr. Kovacevic. This decision dismisses Vahid Ceric from the post of assistant commander for the organisation of mobilisation and personnel appears. Sir, first of all, did you know Vahid Ceric; and, if so, what ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know him very well, but I was acquainted with him, and he was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under the second paragraph of this decision, Major Radmilo Zeljaja is directed to implement this decision --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, and do you know what Major Zeljaja's ethnicity was and what his position was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, we are dealing with two things here: Major Zeljaja was a Serb. And the second thing is that he was a member of the army. And I think it's rather unusual for the Executive Committee to get involved with army issues and to appoint army personnel to positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01739, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, this document last exhibited recites a decision as made pursuant to Article 78 of the rules of procedure, et cetera. I cannot now recall, but I assume that there was a similar recital in terms of the last -- the previous document. Is -- are these rules of procedure of the Executive Committee part, or will become part, of the law library?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, actually, I don't have that question -- the answer to that off the top of my head, but I can certainly check on that and give you the answer at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move on to another document. This is 65 ter 3685.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is in tab 5 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this one is similar to the previous documents, and it's a decision dismissing Iso Bucan from the post of commander for logistics security. And can you tell us what was Mr. Bucan's ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Iso Bucan was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could I tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked. Mr. Dobbyn, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01740.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, I assume that these are tendered as examples of a pattern of what was going on at the time. The -- is there anything -- how long is this list?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I have -- in total, I had six of these documents. There are three left, Your Honours. I can go through them if you'd like, or I could seek to tender them separately later on. There is the following document where he's able to offer specific information about what happened to the person named in that document afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: The next document is 65 ter 3686.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's at tab 6 in the binder. And, sir, in this decision Idriz Jakupovic is dismissed from the post of president of the Prijedor municipal staff for the reception of refugees, and he's to be replaced by Jovan Vukoja. And, again, briefly, could I ask you what the ethnicity of these two individuals was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The gentleman being dismissed is a Bosniak, and the one being appointed is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you know whether Idriz Jakupovic survived the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know - I wanted to add this - Idriz Jakupovic also ended up at Omarska and he died there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01741, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you have noted, these are examples. There were a further two documents. But looking at the time, the time I have left for this witness, I'll move on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know how, and if you intend to approach this and I expect that if you do, the relevant point would be at the time of submissions, but I'm curious as to whether, in terms of the documents that you have tendered, there is a, from the Prosecution's point of view and in terms of the reason why it's relying on these, a difference between the previous documents, which purported to have been done under the provisions of a particular rule, and this which doesn't show any linkage. It's something that perhaps you can flag to return to at the appropriate stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, moving on to a slightly different topic. After the Serb takeover in Prijedor, did you become aware of any arrests taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By all means, the first thing that you hear about were the arrests, the arrests of acquaintances and other people who I didn't know. I heard about the arrests of some of my colleagues and so on. I know that I talked on the telephone with the director of the public audit service and I said that we were worried. We were worried. We wanted to know whether he could hide anywhere. We thought that if we didn't do anything, if we hadn't done anything, if we weren't guilty, we would be safe. However, that wasn't the case. I mentioned the president of town planning, and he was arrested and he was in a camp. Later, when I talked to the director of the revenue service, I could hear something in the background. He said, Hang on a minute. Somebody is ringing the door bell. I'll be back. And he never returned. His wife talked to me on the phone, and she said that the police had been there and they took her husband away. These arrests were really horrific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you have an intervention?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Page 15, line 18, I believe the witness said something in addition which wasn't recorded. Along the lines that this person was not guilty of anything and he wasn't even the member of the party. So maybe this can be clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dobbyn, could you have the witness confirm that he added this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you hear my learned colleague's comments? When talking, I believe, about the president of town planning, did you also say that he was not guilty of anything and wasn't even a member of the party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. What would you like me to explain?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, could you give us the name of the president of town planning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The president of town planning was Senad Mujkanovic. He was a construction engineer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said he was arrested and he was in a camp. Do you know which camp he was in and what happened to him there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that he was at Omarska and he died there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also referred to the arrest of the director of revenue service, who was arrested while you were on the phone with him. Could you tell us his name. And do you know what happened to him; where he was taken and what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The director of the revenue service was Mehmed Tusic. He was with an economist. He was taken to Omarska and killed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, did you actually witness anyone you knew being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the president of the municipality Muhamed Alic get arrested. I saw that the police took him away.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The last name is Cehajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you saw police take him away. Could you tell us how these police were dressed, what uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were uniformed policemen. They were wearing blue police uniforms. Not camouflage ones, but regular police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Mr. Cehajic after he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, after his arrest, either immediately - I don't know that - but I know that he was taken to the Omarska camp. And I know that he disappeared. He was at the mine as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, could you just explain that last comment. You know he disappeared and he was at the mine as well. What did you mean by that exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I said the mine, I meant Omarska. I know that there was a camp at Omarska. And according to some eye-witnesses, he disappeared. A few years after the war I heard that his remains were found and identified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did you know a man named Enes Bajramovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was a colleague of mine. He used to work at the mine, and he was a mechanical engineer. He was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what were the circumstances of his killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was looking for somebody whom he could trust and who could get him out. I once called his parents later on and I talked to his mother, who said that somebody had called him to go out and then he was killed. But later I heard that it was exactly those people whom he had found to get him out that killed him. He paid them money and then they killed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, how did -- how did you avoid being arrested at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I was arrested once, and I was taken to the SJB, to the police station. However, at first, I couldn't notice a system saying that this man had done such and such a thing so he needed to be taken into custody. There was either information by a neighbour or somebody wanted to know how a certain person could live freely. For example, when I saw from the window Muhamed Cehajic being led away, I spent the night at my neighbour's. And I tried to hide in an apartment, in a building, because this apartment was empty. However, I was arrested and taken away. I wanted to remove the battery from my car to be able to listen to the radio and somebody saw me and informed the police. So six policemen came in the afternoon, knocked on my door, and they said that somebody had reported having seen me in town. So I understood this to mean that there needed to be a reason for everybody to be accused. That was in June. I believe it might have been the 11th of June. And when I was at the police station I realized that they had no transportation to take me to Omarska because there was a funeral that day. I believe somebody from the Serbian army had been killed, Karlica or somebody. So somebody from the police came and told me to go home but that I wasn't to leave Prijedor because they would come and get me again. So I hid in another apartment. I wasn't at home. And so many people thought that I had been taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Again, a part of the witness's answer was not recorded in the transcript. It's page 18 - 11, 12, and 13 lines. I believe the witness said: "I couldn't notice a system or," and then he mentioned something about the list of -- non-existing list of the people that needed to be arrested. So maybe you can clarify that. I think it's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you probably heard my learned colleague. If I could just ask you to go back to your answer earlier on. Did you make some mention of a list or a non-existent list of people that needed to be arrested? And, if so, could you repeat what you said about that list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll repeat. What I meant was that there wasn't anything like that. There was no evidence whatsoever, there was no reason whatsoever for the people being taken away. For example, when my colleague from town planning was taken away, they said he had done such and such a thing so we're taking him away. And for the other man, again, they said he had done such and such a thing so we're taking him away. The reason was that they were not Serbs. And then indictments were filed later on. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've described being arrested and taken to the Prijedor police station by some police on one occasion and not being taken to Omarska because there was no police vehicle available. Was this -- during the period that you were in hiding, was this the only time that police confronted you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police also came. Later it was difficult for me to tell the police apart from other forces because the police started wearing camouflage uniforms. However, the police came to my apartment one time to look for weapons, to see if I had any weapons, so they searched the whole apartment. Even my children, who were small, they were born in 1982 and 1987, and they took them into a room and interrogated them. They asked them whether we had any weapons. And for me I considered that to be an abuse of my children. But they didn't find any weapons in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other occasion where you were confronted by the police while you were in an apartment, either your own or the apartment you were hiding in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was in the second apartment, there were some uniformed people. Whether they were police or not, I don't know. But they searched the building, asking whether there were any weapons there. I had very bad experiences at the time, because I was alone in an abandoned apartment and I hid there. One morning I heard terrible banging on the door so I had to open, and when I opened, I saw two uniformed men. I took out my identity card, so they saw that I wasn't the owner of the apartment. One of them wanted to take me downstairs, the other one said to point the rifle at my head. And he left, so I stayed there kneeling with the rifle pointed at my head. After a lot of banging and doors being open, I could hear a sound that I couldn't identify. And after this, the second policeman ran downstairs, grabbed the man who had me at gunpoint, and said to him, Let's run. I went into the apartment. I didn't know what had saved me. But later on I found out that what saved me was that the man who had gone upstairs went to an apartment that was opened by a man who was sick so he lost his patience and he shot him. He had shot the man in the leg, so he started bleeding. He screamed, How could you hit him? He was one of ours; he was a Serb. So he got confused and left. I think that was what saved me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you in hiding for, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And one more thing - I'm sorry - the policemen came for me one more time. That might have been in late July or early August. An American journalist called Guttman was looking for me. So the police took me to the restaurant at the Ljubija mine, and after that I returned to my own apartment. That was when I saw Kovacevic and Drljaca. And Kovacevic's initial reaction was to say to me, I thought you were either dead or at Omarska. That was his reaction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to go back to my previous question. Could you tell me how long you were in hiding for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Look, I was in hiding the whole time. The whole time I was in Prijedor. Because if somebody didn't know that you existed, that was a good thing. I had to hide for a long time, and it's very difficult for me to talk about this. From the takeover of power until I left in late 1992 -- [microphone not activated] ... every day was just waiting. During a walk, one of my younger daughters asked, How can we keep saying this? During that whole time, nobody could know about us. Until we left Bosnia. I had back pain while I was walking around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm interested as to exactly why you felt the need to go into hiding. Obviously you described people being arrested. At that time, in 1992, while in Prijedor, did you hear anything about what was happening to those non-Serbs who were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course, I heard from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- did -- many were killed in the camps. Many were taken away, and many were killed in one way or another. They were either beaten or shot to death. At any rate, the camp was where they met their death. That's why it was important to get out of Prijedor. I even found out about some people who were queuing at the police for their papers to be able to get out. They were taken away from the police station to Keraterm, and there they were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to just quickly touch on something you referred to a while back. You had said there was a proclamation on the radio calling for non-Serbs to return to work. Do you know anyone personally who responded to that call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look, we were so naive and we knew we were completely innocent. We were so naive that my wife told me, Why don't you respond and go to your work? At least we won't have to go on hiding in this apartment. But there was this man I knew who did respond. Of course, he was immediately arrested, taken to the camp, and killed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what his name was and what camp he was taken to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one I mentioned now was Camil Pezo. He was killed in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to another area. And, sir, can you recall an attack on Stari Grad that took place in late May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I was in the apartment which gave a view to a part of the old town, and it was very close to the old town. One morning, it was foggy, I was woken up by the sound of shooting, and it's hard to say how long it lasted, but it was not that long. When I was able to see, I saw a tank with its gun trained at the old town and firing at the old town. I saw the movement of vehicles and uniformed people wearing all sorts of caps, red and other colours. There were all sorts of troops, police, army troops, paramilitaries. When the fog lifted, I was able to see also vehicles carrying dead bodies, like pick-up trucks or flat-bed trucks carrying bodies. But all the people that I could see were civilians. In the old town, on the other side, I couldn't see any shooting, just this tank trained at the old town. Later that same day, on the side where I had a worse view, I saw buses carrying people. And I heard from my neighbours from Zvornik who recognised some of the people getting off the buses, I heard from them they knew some of these people and they were taken later to the camp. Then there were these new buildings, newly opened shops selling small cars and technical goods. I saw people coming with cars to loot. They were so fully loaded after the looting they were no longer able to see through their own back shields. They had to peer out of the window. And when the looting finished, then they started burning houses one by one in the old town. I saw people going into buildings, throwing a grenade in, and then getting out. And then you would see the houses start to burn. In one neighbourhood, I saw them shoot at the house before burning it down. Also, the town mosque faired the same way. They destroyed it. And our main fear was that it might collapse onto the building next door. Later on, some sort of delegation came and was told that the town was destroyed in combat operations, but I knew it was a dirty lie, because I had seen them before, burning houses down one by one. And whatever was not fully destroyed by fire, they destroyed by bringing construction machinery to level them. That's how they destroyed the entire old town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to just explore that in a little more detail some of the points that you've described there. First of all, you had said that you were woken by a sound of gun-fire in the morning on that day. Are you able to recall what time of the morning it was that you were woken by this gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, that was a long time ago, but it was in the morning. I don't know what time in the morning, but it was a very foggy morning. I was hardly able to see out of my window towards the Sana river. It's hard to say what time it was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It has been a long time, so I certainly understand that. Are you able to say how intense this shooting that you heard was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I had to make an estimate, and it would be very rough, it lasted for about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall roughly what time it was that the fog lifted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, I'm sorry to disturb, but it seems we lost the B/C/S translation here. And we are back, I guess, now. I would kindly invite the counsel to repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, I'll repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall roughly what time it was that the fog lifted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the fog lifted and it became much clearer around 8.00. I was able to see outside. I think it was around that time that the fog lifted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also described a tank that was shelling the Stari Grad area. At the time that the tank was shelling that area, was there any gun-fire going on then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, from what I was able to see, it was a tank that fired. As for cannons, I did not see that. So I cannot say anything positive about that. I just saw the tower of the mosque was shot at. Maybe those were guns or Howitzers, but I could see that some sort of artillery hit the mosque tower. Whether it was a hand-operated cannon or a different cannon, I don't know that. But there was this tank firing at the old town and hitting targets very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, you have about a minute left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I believe that we had started the questioning at around about quarter past. But in any case, I would -- I have just a few more questions, and I would ask for a maximum of another 15 minutes to finish up this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: 15. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I wasn't very clear with my question. You said that you were woken by shooting outside. What I'm asking is that when the shelling from the tank started, was the shooting still going on, or had the shooting stopped at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that gun-fire that woke me up was a bit more intensive than later. In fact, later, there was no shooting of the same kind. There was gun-fire from some other place that I could not see, but it was not intensive fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when the fog cleared, did you see any Green Berets or armed Muslims fleeing the old town area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could certainly not see that. I did not see anyone in uniform except the army troops, the police, and the paramilitaries of the Serbian army. All the people I saw on trucks and in other vehicles. In fact, the dead bodies I saw were all in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any civilians in the old town area putting up any armed resistance to the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see a single armed civilian offering any resistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned looting taking place. Was it uniformed people who were -- who were doing this looting, or was this civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was done by uniformed people. They went into houses and shops, emptied them, looting. I don't think civilians had access to those places at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to tell whether those looting were army, paramilitary, or police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was very difficult for me to discern who wore what kind of uniform. I could just see that there were various uniforms and even a variety of berets. There were some red berets worn by men who came from Banija [Realtime transcript read in error "Banja"], then there were greener uniforms, or at least not so blue as the police uniforms. But which units, which branch they belonged to, I could not tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see police uniforms, police uniforms that you recognised as police uniforms in the Stari Grad area?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I -- I believe the witness clearly explained in his previous answer that he was unable to distinguish whether this -- these uniforms belongs to -- belonged to whichever branch of -- or unit. So I don't see the basis for this question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, earlier on he said very specifically that he has seen police in the old town area during the time of this attack. I'm simply trying to clarify this for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, after -- after Mr. Dobbyn instructed the witness, I don't see what is -- what will be the value of his answer now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The witness did say that "there were greener uniforms, or at least not so blue as the police uniforms." And that would suggest that perhaps in some of those operations there might have been people wearing blue uniforms. And that's what the question goes to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would gladly ask that the -- this audiotape be verified. Because the witness himself said, I couldn't distinct to which unit these people belonged to. There were different kinds of uniforms, and I couldn't distinct to which kind of unit they belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the fact that there seems to be some lack of clarity between the people in the courtroom themselves is all the more reason to try and clarify this with the witness. We want this to be clear for the record, and so that's why I'm exploring it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The only objections that I think that could have been made is that the way that the question which prompted Mr. Zecevic's rising was that it was a leading question. But that apart, clearly it is a matter which should be clarified. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've described several different groups of people who were in the old town area during this attack, during the looting and the burning of the houses. Were you able to positively tell that there were people who were police in the old town area at that time; and, if so, how were you able to recognise them as police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That they were members of the police, I could tell about certain people, certain units that were either driving in police cars or who wore distinctly police uniforms. But at a later stage there were so many camouflage uniforms, combat and military camouflage uniforms, that I could not recognise which ones were army troops or paramilitaries. Some were White Eagles; others wore red berets. The police I could distinguish, especially on one side, looking on one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry, one correction: Page 27, line 16, the witness mentioned the Red Berets had come from Banija. "Banija." The transcript says "Banja," and it should be B-a-n-i-j-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, if we could look at 65 ter 3683. And this is in tab 16 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, is this another topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: No. This is on the same topic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what you see in front of you is a photograph that was taken on 24 September 1995. Do you recognise the area shown in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I recognise this area. But this image shows the outcome of what the Serb forces did. This cleared forest is an area -- this clearing is a place where, in other times, there used to be many, many houses. This is the bridge on the Sana river; facing it, the hotel; and then the old town. The whole old town was cleared.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to check whether the witness is able to mark the hard copy of the photograph he has in front of him. If so, I'd like him to draw a circle around the area he has said is the -- where the old town stood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can hear from -- oh, I see that it is being marked. I'm sorry, I can see now that it is being marked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can draw the number 1 in the centre of that circled area, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you can see the area that I believe you described as Stari Grad is completely bare. Can you give an estimate of how many houses were standing in that area in Stari Grad before the attack in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very densely populated. The houses stood very close together. There was certainly a couple of thousand, several thousand population, but how many exactly, it's hard to say. But there were a lot of people, and the houses stood very close to one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the building that you are hiding in and from which you observed the attack shown in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for our sake over here, can you describe which building you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I mark it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please. If you could mark it with the number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We are not getting the markings, Your Honour. How do we understand what is the -- the number 1, what is the number 2, if we don't see it? How can we cross-examine the witness on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: After he marks it, I'll be asking him to explain which building it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And to the extent that it works, perhaps he can hold it up to the camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'll have him do that once I've finished with the markings which he performs, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you've marked that building with number 2, can you please describe which building it is in the photo so that we here in The Hague will be able to know which one you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Shall I turn it towards the camera? Perhaps that would be best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. If you could do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Old town. Old town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, is that coming up? We're not seeing it on ours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The house, the building where I was...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Is that coming up for anyone else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can he show --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Can we please -- sorry, Your Honours, we don't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the area of the old town was this, all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honours, we're seeing the witness's face at the moment. Is this going out? because -- no. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the area of the old town. The building from which I watched this is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would it be a suggestion to have that marked on -- on the document we have now on the screen? I mean, we clearly saw what the witness indicated, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So that's solved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is just one other marking I'd like you to make, sir. And this is -- you described earlier that there was a -- you saw a tank shelling Stari Grad. Could you mark with the number 3 where you saw that tank? And then when you've finished that, if you could hold it up to the camera and point that out again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tank was standing here, roughly. Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just want to make sure, before I ask for this photograph to be admitted, that can you confirm that you have clearly marked, first of all, the Stari Grad area with the number 1; the apartment you were observing the attack from with the number 2; and the location of the tank with the number 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, I would like to tender this photograph with its markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and that concludes -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01742.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And that concludes my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Which brings us to the break. We will adjourn and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I had a follow-up question already before Mr. Krgovic addressed the issue. Mr. Witness, you talked about the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You talked about the Red Berets from Banija. What did you mean by that? Who were they, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, those were some formations from the battle-grounds in Croatia in Banija. I don't know where they had originally been formed, but those were the Serbs wearing red berets, at least that's what some people told me, and that they were the Serb formations that had come from the battle-fields in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, if I may, before you begin your cross-examination. The Chamber has received a motion filed yesterday from the Prosecution in respect of a witness who is to testify on Monday, seeking protective measures. And we would be grateful if, by tomorrow, we could have responses from the Defence to this motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm already -- I'm ready to give my response later today. When we finish with this witness, maybe that would be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Aleksic, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: With regard to the events of the 30th of April, you testified in the Stakic case as well, and you mentioned it today also. On page 2480, you said that on that day you stayed at home, that you did not venture out, and that you spoke with Mr. Talundzic over the phone who told you not to go to work. Did Mr. Talundzic tell you that -- or before, that -- anything about a meeting held on the 29th of April, 1992, at the Prijedor SJB, which was attended by Mr. Simo Miskovic, the president of the SDS, and Mr. Mirza Mujadzic from the SDA, in addition to the people from the SJB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me what I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm asking you about the meeting of the 29th of April. Did he tell you anything about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Talundzic tell you anything about the dispatches sent on that day, the 29th of April, by the republican MUP from Mr. Delimustafic, as well as from the republican TO Staff from Mr. Hasan Efendic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on that day, the 29th of April, pursuant to an order issued by the two above-mentioned gentlemen, Efendic and Delimustafic, the MUP and TO defence units were ordered to enter into combat operations into the entire territory of B and H?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On pages 2485 and 86 in the Stakic case, you said that after the 30th of April your access to information was restricted, which meant that you could listen to the radio very seldom because it was a battery-operated radio. And you mentioned the same thing today. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Also in the Stakic case, on page 22 -- 2600, you said that after 30th of April there was a period of calm which lasted for about two or three weeks. Then on pages 2601 and 02, you added that after the takeover of April [as interpreted] on the 30th of April you remained in your flat until you learned that Mr. Cehajic was arrested, which happened towards the end of May 1992. Do you remember that; and do you remember mentioning it today as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period, were you able to hear on the radio that on the 22nd of May a check-point in Hambarine was attacked? The check-point that was manned by the JNA troops.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that there were some attacks. I know that immediately after the takeover of power two men were killed, but I also remember that there was mention of this attack on the check-point. However, the two men killed in Vozicini [phoen] were Bosniaks. However, nobody mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And do you know if Mr. Cehajic and some other persons were arrested after the 23rd of May in the wake of the attack on the soldiers in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know about Cehajic. Some were arrested before him; some were arrested after him. Not all the people were arrested on the same day. Some were arrested earlier; some were arrested later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Concerning the event of the 30th of May and the attack on Prijedor, you said that on that morning there was fog and that shots could be heard coming from all sides. You said that on page 2494 in the Stakic case also. On page 2696, you said that later on you heard on the radio that the destruction was caused by combat operations. And then, on page 2588, you were asked the following question. [In English] [Previous translation continues] "Are you aware of the attack on Prijedor of the end of May 1992? "I heard that, in the building I was in, that neighbours later said that the group had carried out an attack somewhere, but I don't know anything about the details. I was in apartment in one room of that apartment. "Did you hear the shooting on the 30th May, 1992? "Yes. Shooting was heard, could be heard." [Interpretation] Do you remember giving this evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was there a question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with what I read, and is it consistent with your evidence in the Stakic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Again, in the Stakic case, and I believe you mentioned the same thing today, you said that from your room you could only see one part of the old town. Tell me, from the position where you were, were you able to see the bridge across the Sana?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see the bridge. And one can see that from the map that I showed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Had you heard that parts of units led by Slavko Ecimovic carried out an attack on Prijedor by crossing the bridge across the Sana towards the old town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear where they crossed. I heard shooting aimed at some group that carried out an attack, but I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions for you. Can you tell me, you mentioned listening to the radio for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that was your main source of information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One of the sources of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Muharem Nezirovic was the editor of Radio Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Until he went to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That means up until June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know when, but I know that he ended up in Omarska, and I saw him live here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mean after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I tell that Mr. Nezirovic was the editor of Radio Prijedor throughout April and May ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you're saying is not interesting at all. We could only hear about Mutic. We didn't hear anything from Nezirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, whether it's interesting or not is a completely different issue. Of course you were not able to hear him because this gentleman was editor-in-chief of Radio Prijedor and he was not a broadcaster. Now, could you confirm and can you allow for a possibility that Mr. Nezirovic was the editor-in-chief of radio Prijedor throughout April and May? Can you confirm that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot, because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you listened to the radio, do you remember that a certain lady named Senija Dzafic was a news reader?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never heard her name. I know that she only read out what was signed by Mutic. By Mutic and a certain man called Kesar [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you were able to hear Ms. Senija Dzafic as a news reader on radio Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what her name was, but I know that what she was reading was signed by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I think we should be going into private session, or at least this last question should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have a further question which require us to move into private session, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I posed the question in a manner which I didn't expect this answer, but ... well, to be on the safe side, maybe it's better that we are, for a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, a while ago, in response to the question posed by my learned friend, you said that you were not familiar with the order on the commencement of war operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina issued by Messrs. Cengic and Delimustafic dated the 24th of April. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I said Cengic, but I was referring to Mr. Hasan Efendic. Tell me, do you know that way back on the 25th of April the commander of the TO Staff was nominated for the area of Puharska and that was done by Mr. Hasan Cengic [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I absolutely know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Puharska is a region near Prijedor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a Jusuf Ramic from Puharska who was appointed commander on the 25th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with that name at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on that same day the Kozarac TO commander became a certain Mr. Madunjanin by appointment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where was he appointed to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He was appointed commander of the TO Staff of the Patriotic League for the Kozarac sector.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that. When you mentioned Puharska, I just know that the -- that the mosque was mined there and the Catholic church in town. That's what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with Muharem Handanagic [phoen], a colonel from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you're referring to a municipal official, he might have been in the reserve. I know the man. I'm acquainted with him. He was murdered in his apartment or his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that he was appointed commander of the TO Staff, that is, of the Patriotic League, for the entire territory of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. As for him, I just know that he was murdered in his yard, as a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. My learned friend showed you two documents which you commented on. Just a moment. Those were tabs 4 and 5. The first document is 65 ter 3684. That's tab 4. I apologise, I know it was given an exhibit number, but I was not able to write it down. Do you remember that you commented on this document earlier today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Among others, you said that it is interesting that Major Zeljaja, as a military personnel, is mentioned here is -- is interesting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it's true, is it not, that the commander for the organisation of mobilisation and personnel affairs is a part of the National Defence sector in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me say just this: That's more of a legal issue. I know that some people - there might have been two people - who were on the municipal budget. They were in the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As vice-president of the Executive Committee of the municipality, I'm certain that you knew that there is a municipal organ in charge of National Defence. That's how it was laid down in the laws of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the people who worked in the National Defence organs and the whole National Defence system was under the JNA. At least it was a part of the JNA. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Secretariat for National Defence was a part of the municipality, a part of the Executive Committee. Now, as for which part was in the army, I'm not certain. For those things that we were uncertain about, we called a secretary who was a lawyer and who was in charge of the statute and then we would act in accordance with what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You must know that the JNA, which was the basic defence force of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, had to give its consent for the appointment of any employee in the municipal sectors of National Defence. You must know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. The Secretariat for National Defence and the chief, I don't think that the army had anything to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Major Radmilo Zeljaja was a member of the JNA, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He was in the Prijedor garrison; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On page 18 of today's transcript -- let me just paraphrase exactly what you said. I intervened because your answer wasn't recorded in its entirety. You said: I was arrested once, detained, that is, and I was taken to the public security station, the police station. As far as I could tell, I didn't notice that there was a system? And then you said, Nor that there was a list according to which people were taken into custody. Instead - and this is what the transcript says: A man would do something and then he needed to be taken into custody. Let's just clarify this, because your answer wasn't recorded. If I understood you correctly, you said that your impression at the time was that there wasn't a system and that there wasn't a list according to which people were taken into custody, and that, instead, this was done ad hoc, or this was because a neighbour would report somebody. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I said. I would just like to add that we asked why people were being taken away, and nobody could give us an indictment for a person who was taken away. Accusations were later fabricated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that, sir? How -- where did you get that information, that accusations or indictments were later fabricated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we heard later from some people that people were being asked about things that they knew nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it's a fact that the first time you were taken into custody you were asked by the inspectors at the police station whether it was true that on that day you were walking around town wearing a uniform. Wasn't that the question they asked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was accused of having been seen in town in a uniform. And I didn't dare walk around town in any sort of clothing, let alone a uniform. That was just a fabrication. Somebody had called in and said that I was seen in a uniform. That was a fabrication; it was a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree that it's a lie. I'm not saying that you were walking around Prijedor in a uniform. It would never cross my mind to say something like that. What I'm asking you is: Your testimony is that somebody called the police station and said, Such and such a person - I don't want to mention a name - was seen today walking around Prijedor wearing a uniform. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The second time, when you had an incident with some uniformed people and you don't know whether they were policemen but you assumed that they were, was when you opened your front door. Do you remember you talked about this? And then a weapon was pointed at your head.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion, when you showed your identity card, they were able to see that you were neither the owner of the apartment nor did you have residence at that address. That's why they pointed the weapon at you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, they could see that it wasn't a Serbian name; and, second of all, they could see that my last name didn't match the name on the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this was in July and August, if I remember your testimony correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As for that second apartment, I don't know when that was. I just know that it happened in that second apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that earlier today you said that this was in July or August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Because in July or August I was taken away by the police, when -- when Guttman wanted to see me. That was earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this event was in June or July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It must -- it might have been June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you will agree with me that in both these cases - when you were taken into custody to the police station and the second time, when they pointed a weapon at you - that on both those occasions, there was some grounds for them to suspect that something was not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether there were grounds, I don't know. But I know that there were Serbian snipers on that building, and I don't know why they were searching the building on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, that apartment where the two men found you when you opened the door, you had gone into that apartment because it was abandoned. It wasn't your apartment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that you heard from the neighbours in the hallway, you heard them talking. Were they Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And these neighbours knew that you were in that apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They saw me only once and that was earlier. I said that this man had asked me to be in that apartment. He had been their neighbour, and he had left Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Either way, sir, when, in July or August, this policeman called you in to meet with the journalist --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may I suggest that we go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1998, you gave a statement to the OTP; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly. I don't know which year. There was a number of statements that I gave. Different occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You gave one on the 14th through 16 August 1997. And this must be the second one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, at that time in 1998, you said that on that occasion you did not recognise a single soldier or a policeman in that place. And you were talking about that attack, that conflict, around the old town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean as I would recognise somebody that I knew?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you because earlier this morning not everything was quite clear about your answer. And you were even questioned by the Trial Chamber whether you had seen people in police uniforms that day, the 30th of May. Because your evidence is that you had seen people in a variety of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm asking you: On that day, did you see a single person that you can say was a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's true that there was a variety of uniforms that I still don't know to whom they belong. But where it was less visible, where there were civilians and people were getting off, there I could see some people in police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just explain something to you. What you are saying is interpreted and then recorded, so occasionally, because of that procedure, parts of your answer do not find their way into the record. I need to clear this up. You said just now that what you saw were several policemen around the buses when people were getting onto those buses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have before you the photograph, P1742?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean that map?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This photograph of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, approximately, where those buses that you had seen were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That side was less visible. They were on the other side, in this lower part of the picture, if I can put it that way. Those streets at the bottom of the picture. There's another exit from the old town where civilians were able to leave, and I could not see all of them. I could see just one part of the column, near the buses. How many buses there were, I couldn't see. I couldn't see whether there were more of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly now, on the side where your apartment was facing you could not see the area where people were getting onto buses because it's on the opposite side of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw one section; perhaps one end of it. I couldn't see how many buses there were. I could just see those that were on one end. The front end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you were giving that statement in 1997 and 1998, you confirmed that you had not seen the people who were injured or dead being carried away after the conflict around the old town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just saw those people laid out on trucks being driven away. Where, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the corpses of people killed, on the trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did they have no tarpaulin, these trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tarpaulin was very loose. Sometimes it did not really cover the trucks. So you could easily see inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you see those trucks with dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were driving along the road. I don't know where they were headed. I -- I saw them driving by.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Along which road --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just let me finish the question. Take it easy. You mentioned a road. Which road? Is that the road where the tank was standing, facing the Sana bridge, or some other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was this road just outside the building. You can see a road just outside the building that connects with this road heading for the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And from the window of that apartment you saw trucks driving by, past the building; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You had some friends who lived in the old town; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that man can barely walk now from all that he's suffered in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact, sir, isn't it, that while you were in Prijedor you did not see a single killing; you heard about all of that from other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And all this information that you shared with us about certain persons, all this is hearsay, isn't it? All that you heard about the fate of some people who lost their lives or were arrested, all this is information you got from other people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
