utterances.text: I do just have a few questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were asked by my learned colleague, Mr. Aleksic, about Mr. Cehajic's arrest, and it was put to you that he was arrested after the incident at the Hambarine check-point. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, up until the point where -- when Mr. Cehajic was arrested, did you have any contact or regular contact with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we were trying to keep a low profile, to stay at home, because we didn't know the intentions of the new authorities. We sometimes had contact, but very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, it was put to you by my learned colleague that you must have maintained close contact with SDA party leadership. So I would like to ask you: With the contact that you did have with him, did he ever discuss with you organising any armed resistance to the takeover in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In -- all the contacts with the president of the municipality were business contacts concerning the establishment and the organisation of the municipality itself, and there was never any mention of any military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: After the takeover, did you ever have any discussions with Mr. Cehajic about how you should react to the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we talked, and I already said that we were very naive, because we thought that we were innocent so we had nothing to be afraid of, and why should we leave? We thought we were safe remaining at home. But, as I said, it was a very naive outlook.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked - and this is at transcript page 36 - about whether you had heard on the radio that damage in the old town area was caused by combat operations. And you were also asked whether your Serb neighbours had said that a group had carried out an attack on Prijedor on that day. Do you recall being asked those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask you, just to clarify: Your observations of what happened in the old town area on the 30th of May, was that consistent with combat operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I heard, and from the official version, that was not consistent with what I saw. On the radio, they said the devastation was a result of military combat operations, but I saw something entirely different. What they said on the radio was a pure lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, on -- on the same subject of what you'd heard on the radio, Mr. Zecevic asked you about the editor in-chief of the radio, Mr. Nezirovic, and you had responded that you only heard Mutic, not Nezirovic. And just to clarify, could you just tell the Trial Chamber who Mutic was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were two: There was the director of Radio Prijedor Mile Mutic, and there was Rade Mutic, journalist of the "Kozara Vjesnik." Both of them worked hard on the propaganda, sowing hatred against non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: In this period following the takeover, what was the nature of the broadcast on Radio Prijedor? Would you consider them to have been balanced, or, rather, were they one-sided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I listened to Prijedor while saving my battery, but what I heard was one-sided; mainly proclamations of the Crisis Staff. I didn't need to listen to a lot of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: You were also asked some questions about the incidents when you were arrested or confronted by police or other armed people, and it was suggested to you that in both cases there was a basis for those confrontations. Now, first of all, the apartment that you were hiding in, who owned that apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the apartment of a relative of mine who was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: It was put to you that, as I said, the police were justified or had a basis for these confrontations with you. Now, you described an incident where a man in the same building, a Serb man, was shot in the leg. From what you heard from the neighbours and from what you observed at that time, did there appear to be any justification for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my view, there was absolutely no justification. However, I heard later that raids were made in other buildings as well. They were searched. They were looking for weapons or armed men. But, as I said, in my building, such an operation was absolutely unnecessary, because there were Serbian snipers on the rooftop, and it was pointless in every way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there any justification for the arrests of those other non-Serb persons that you named earlier on in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think this calls for speculation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning all the persons I know and that I mentioned, there was absolutely no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, it was also put to you at the end of the questioning from my learned colleague that everything that you testified to regarding arrests and so forth was pure hearsay. But, just to confirm, again, isn't it the case that you were actually an eye-witness to the arrest of Mr. Cehajic? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the attack on Prijedor Stari Grad, old town, is referred to as around end of May. Do you know of the exact date of that attack you witnessed from your apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't tell you the exact date. I think it was the second half of or the end of May. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do you know about what is referred to as the Muslim attack on Prijedor? More or less in that same period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about that. I know only what I could hear from Radio Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And did you hear on Radio Prijedor about a Muslim attack on Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I am talking about the radio, I mean to say that they would have kept the population mobilised. They were already talking about the existence of Green Berets, Muslim units, that could attack at any moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I wanted to have some clarification about what you were telling us on the arrest of people and on the absence or not of system and lists. Is it your testimony that those arrests were individual actions by individual policemen, paramilitary, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, there must have been individual cases, of course, but most of the arrests were made by the police. I know of colleagues from the mine, for instance, one was a Croat - most of the arrests were of non-Serbs or perhaps some people were arrested because they wanted their apartments. But a large number of people went missing in one way or another. One number of people would be arrested on one day, and then it would be the turn of others. One of my colleagues who went missing, a mechanical engineer, as he was getting ready, he said, In my building, no one knows on which night they will hear the knock on the door. It was like with the Russian Gulag arrests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You say, "most of the arrests were of non-Serbs or perhaps some people were arrested because they wanted their apartments." Do you know of any Serbs being arrested on the basis of what you call phone calls, phone calls to the police, to give them information that you say was fabricated for one or the other reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't give you a single example of an arrested Serb. Perhaps if they found somebody of their own, unsuitable or unloyal, they could have become a target too. But all the people I can talk about are -- they're all non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, sorry, just one correction to the transcript. One part of the witness's answer is missing. When he said most of those arrested - that's page 59, line 12. When he says, [In English] that a large number of people -- a number of people would be arrested on another date -- [no interpretation] ... arrested because they wanted their apartment [Interpretation] and when he talks about they were arrested because they wanted their apartments. And one sentence is missing: Or on the basis of a neighbour's denunciation. Do you agree, witness, that you said they there were also arrested based on neighbour's denunciations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Some denunciations came from neighbours too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. And we thank the witness for his assistance to the Tribunal. Sir, you are now released. Thank you. And we thank the Court Officer for his assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, does the Prosecution have another witness available today?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: No, sorry, Your Honours, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But you do have a witness available for tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, we do. There's a witness who I believe is in The Hague at the moment or arriving today, but not available to start at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what about Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you know, the witness originally scheduled for Monday has had the medical problem. I'm told he's recovering well. He seemed in good spirits. Did talk about the possibility of still wanting to come forward and testify, but we're not certain he'll be ready to testify on Friday. We certainly have one more witness for tomorrow, but that may be the only witness that we're going to be able to put on the rest of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: When you say "one more," you mean in addition to the scheduled witnesses, or the scheduled witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The scheduled witness for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And possibly the one who was scheduled for Monday could go on Friday, but I think it's highly unlikely. I would feel uncomfortable doing that, given what's transpired with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic, you indicated that you would be in a position to respond to the motion before we rise for the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, if I may now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the position of the -- of the Stanisic Defence is that we oppose the -- the request. I just made the analysis, Your Honours. I will very briefly say. I just made the analysis: Almost 50 per cent of the witnesses that were heard in this trial had one or the other kind of the protective measure. Now, in the last couple of instances, I -- I seem to recall - and I believer my recollection is right - that -- that the witnesses are now talking about not -- not -- not actual threats or anything of the kind but assumptions that -- things like that might happen due to different reasons. And because of that, we don't feel that it -- that this application meets the threshold to give the protective measures to that witness. And we are very concerned about the -- the number of the witnesses which -- which have been granted the protective measures because we believe that -- it is my honest belief that there might be some other reason why -- why this -- why this is -- why this is requested and not really the -- the -- the problem or the threat to -- to the -- to body and -- or of that witness or his family. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would say, although we're not ready to rule immediately, that the Chamber shares the concern that you have. Does the -- sorry, does the Zupljanin Defence have a response?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's a joint submission by Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will consider this and probably rule -- well, we would have to rule tomorrow. So we rise for the day, to resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of December, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
